title: Low back and leg pain in a 44-year-old (clinic)

patient.name: Dana Whitfield
patient.chiefComplaint: Low back pain for three weeks, now shooting down the left leg
patient.setting: Primary care / urgent care clinic, seated on the exam table

persona.affect: In pain and restless: shifts position often and sometimes stands to ease her leg; practical, direct and good-humoured despite it
persona.speakingStyle: Plain, matter-of-fact everyday words; fairly brief answers, a little clipped when the leg flares; no medical jargon
persona.worries: Losing work time and pay (she is already on light duties); afraid she has done something serious and will need an operation
persona.background: Warehouse supervisor whose job involves lifting; lives with her partner and their two teenagers; enjoys gardening and watching her kids' sports

doorSign.task: Ms. Whitfield, 44, presents with three weeks of low back pain that now shoots down her left leg. Take a focused history, perform a focused back and lower-limb neurological examination, then present your summary, differential diagnosis and initial plan.

doorInstructions.reasonForVisit: Low back pain going down the leg
doorInstructions.task: Take a focused history and perform a focused physical examination. Share your impressions with the patient before you leave. You will then write a post-encounter note.

history.openingStatement: My lower back's been bad for a few weeks, and now I've got this pain shooting down my left leg. It's really getting me down.

facts.topic: Onset of back and leg pain
facts.answer: My back started about three weeks ago — I woke up stiff and sore the morning after helping a friend move a sofa. The pain down my left leg started about ten days ago.

general_appearance.default: Well-looking woman in obvious discomfort: sits tilted onto her right buttock, shifts position every minute or so and stands partway through to ease her leg. Alert and conversant; not otherwise unwell or distressed.

back_inspection.default: Stands with her weight shifted onto the right leg. Spine straight with no scoliosis or lateral shift; the normal lumbar curve is slightly flattened, with prominent left lower paraspinal muscles (spasm). Shoulders and iliac crests level; no skin changes, scars or swelling.

spine_lumbar.text: Tender over the left paraspinal muscles at the lumbosacral junction (around L5–S1), with palpable muscle spasm. No midline spinous process tenderness and no step-off.

response.say: Ooh, that's sore — just there on the left.

back_palpation.sacrum: No tenderness over the sacrum or either sacroiliac joint.

spine_lumbar.text: Forward flexion limited: fingertips reach only mid-thigh before pain shoots down the left leg. Extension mildly painful in the low back. Side-bending and rotation slightly limited by low-back stiffness.

expectedDifferential.diagnosis: Left S1 radiculopathy from an L5–S1 disc herniation
expectedDifferential.rationale: Leg-dominant pain in an S1 distribution (left buttock, back of thigh and calf, lateral foot and little toe) beginning after a lifting and twisting strain; worse with sitting, bending, coughing and sneezing; better lying with knees bent. Positive left straight leg raise at about 40° (crossed SLR negative), reduced left ankle reflex, weak left plantarflexion (cannot toe-walk) and reduced sensation over the lateral foot. Knee reflexes, dorsiflexion and great-toe extension are normal, so L4 and L5 are spared. No red flags: conservative care (analgesia, staying active, review), with imaging if red flags appear, weakness progresses or symptoms persist beyond about 6 weeks.

expectedDifferential.diagnosis: Lumbar muscle strain (mechanical low back pain)
expectedDifferential.rationale: Lifting onset and left paraspinal tenderness and spasm fit, but a strain does not explain dermatomal pain below the knee, sensory loss, a reduced ankle reflex or plantarflexion weakness.

expectedDifferential.diagnosis: Lumbar spinal stenosis (lateral recess or foraminal)
expectedDifferential.rationale: Can compress a single root, but is typically seen in older patients, with leg symptoms brought on by walking and eased by sitting or bending forward; here sitting and flexion worsen the pain and walking helps.
Buttock pain radiating down the leg and worse with sitting, but a reduced reflex, myotomal weakness, dermatomal sensory loss and a positive SLR point to a nerve root lesion.
Can cause buttock and posterior thigh pain, but there is no sacroiliac tenderness, FABER is negative and pain below the knee with neurological deficits is not explained.

expectedDifferential.diagnosis: Must not miss: cauda equina syndrome
expectedDifferential.rationale: Considered and screened for: no urinary retention or incontinence, no bowel change, no saddle numbness, no sexual dysfunction, unilateral symptoms and no bilateral weakness. Safety-net: any of these developing needs same-day emergency assessment and urgent MRI.

expectedDifferential.diagnosis: Must not miss: spinal infection or malignancy
expectedDifferential.rationale: No fever, weight loss, cancer history, night or rest pain, injecting drug use or steroid use, a clear mechanical precipitant and normal vitals make these unlikely.

itemsNotApplicable.reason: A full sexual history is not relevant to this mechanical back and leg pain presentation; new sexual dysfunction is screened as part of the cauda equina red flags.
Travel history is not relevant to this mechanical back and leg pain presentation.
